mcqs.q: The two broad types of drug interaction are:
mcqs.explain: Interactions are classified as drug-drug and drug-food; the more medications taken, the greater the risk.

mcqs.q: Taking hydrocodone with the sedating antihistamine diphenhydramine causes:
mcqs.explain: Both drugs cause drowsiness, so taken together they produce an additive sedative effect.

mcqs.q: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones have reduced ABSORPTION when taken with:
opts: Calcium, iron, antacids or dairy products (chelation)
mcqs.explain: These antibiotics chelate (form insoluble complexes) with calcium, iron, antacids and dairy, reducing their absorption.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs increase the bleeding risk of warfarin during DISTRIBUTION by:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs compete for albumin binding and displace warfarin, raising the free (active) warfarin level and bleeding risk.

mcqs.q: Metronidazole increases warfarin's anticoagulant effect by:
mcqs.explain: Metronidazole inhibits the CYP450 metabolism of warfarin, causing excessive anticoagulation and bleeding risk.

mcqs.q: Rifampicin reduces the efficacy of antifungals and corticosteroids because it:
opts: Induces hepatic enzymes, speeding their metabolism
mcqs.explain: Rifampicin is a strong CYP450 inducer; it accelerates the metabolism of many drugs, lowering their levels and efficacy.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs can cause methotrexate toxicity by:
opts: Reducing renal prostaglandin synthesis and methotrexate clearance
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins and renal clearance of methotrexate, raising its level toward toxicity (an elimination interaction).

mcqs.q: Combining opioids with benzodiazepines or alcohol produces:
mcqs.explain: These are all CNS depressants; together they additively/synergistically enhance sedation and respiratory depression.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs combined with corticosteroids increase the risk of:
mcqs.explain: Both irritate the GI mucosa, so together NSAIDs and corticosteroids raise the risk of GI ulcer and bleeding.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs interact ANTAGONISTICALLY with antihypertensives, leading to:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs antagonise antihypertensives (β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, diuretics), worsening blood-pressure control.

mcqs.q: To avoid the chelation interaction, ciprofloxacin/tetracycline should be given:
opts: 2 hours before or 6 hours after the mineral/dairy/antacid
mcqs.explain: Separate the antibiotic from minerals/dairy/antacids — give it 2 hours before or 6 hours after — or stop unnecessary supplements.

mcqs.q: Which statement about food and drug bioavailability is correct?
opts: Food can also INCREASE bioavailability (e.g. cefuroxime 52% with food vs 37% fasting)
mcqs.explain: Food effects vary: it can reduce some drugs but increase others — cefuroxime is 52% bioavailable with food vs 37% fasting.

mcqs.q: Ampicillin taken with oral contraceptives may cause:
opts: Failure of contraception — advise an alternative method
mcqs.explain: Some antibiotics (e.g. ampicillin) can reduce contraceptive efficacy; patients should be advised to use an alternative method.

mcqs.q: Metronidazole given with lithium causes:
mcqs.explain: Metronidazole decreases lithium excretion, raising lithium levels toward toxicity.

mcqs.q: In a patient taking PROPRANOLOL, adrenaline (in local anaesthetic) can cause:
mcqs.explain: With non-selective β-blockade by propranolol, the adrenaline in local anaesthetic can produce unopposed α-vasoconstriction and a rise in blood pressure.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs taken with ciprofloxacin can lead to:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs can enhance the CNS toxicity of ciprofloxacin, increasing the risk of seizures.

mcqs.q: Therapeutically IMPORTANT interactions are those that:
opts: Alter the intended response, cause toxicity, or alter nutritional status
mcqs.explain: Important interactions alter the intended response, cause drug toxicity, or alter normal nutritional status.

mcqs.q: Which patient is at GREATER risk of food-nutrient-drug interactions?
opts: An elderly, malnourished patient with chronic disease
A healthy young adult on no medication
A patient taking a single short course of antibiotics
A patient using only topical creams
mcqs.explain: At-risk groups include the elderly, malnourished, chronically ill, pregnant women, the fetus and infants.

mcqs.q: A drug that triggers an interaction is the 'precipitant'; the drug whose effect is altered is the:
mcqs.explain: In an interaction, the precipitant drug alters the handling/effect of the object drug.

mcqs.q: Enzyme INDUCTION (e.g. by rifampicin) generally:
opts: Decreases the level and effect of the affected drug
Increases the level of the affected drug
mcqs.explain: Induction speeds metabolism, lowering the affected drug's level and effect; inhibition does the opposite (raising the level).

mcqs.q: Which is the correct example of an ABSORPTION interaction?
mcqs.explain: Tetracycline chelating with calcium in dairy is an absorption interaction; the others involve distribution or metabolism.

mcqs.q: The best general strategy to prevent drug interactions is to:
opts: Evaluate all medications, know famous interactions, and take a full drug history
Prescribe as many drugs as possible
mcqs.explain: Awareness — evaluating medications, knowing famous interactions, grouping medications and listening to the patient's full drug history — prevents most interactions.

saqs.q: Give one drug-interaction example at each pharmacokinetic step (absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination).
saqs.a: Absorption: tetracycline + dairy (chelation). Distribution: NSAIDs displace warfarin from albumin. Metabolism: metronidazole inhibits warfarin (CYP450). Elimination: NSAIDs ↓ methotrexate clearance.

saqs.q: Differentiate additive/synergistic and antagonistic pharmacodynamic interactions with examples.
saqs.a: Additive/synergistic: opioids + benzodiazepines → respiratory depression. Antagonistic: NSAIDs antagonise antihypertensives → poor BP control.

saqs.q: How should tetracycline/quinolones be timed relative to minerals and dairy, and why?
saqs.a: Give the drug 2 h before or 6 h after the mineral/dairy/antacid, because they form insoluble chelate complexes that reduce absorption.

saqs.q: List three dentally-relevant drug interactions and their effects.
saqs.a: Metronidazole + warfarin → bleeding; propranolol + adrenaline (LA) → ↑ BP; ampicillin + contraceptives → contraceptive failure.

saqs.q: What does enzyme inhibition vs induction do to an affected drug's level?
saqs.a: Inhibition raises the affected drug's level (e.g. metronidazole + warfarin). Induction lowers it (e.g. rifampicin + corticosteroids).

saqs.q: Which patient groups are at greatest risk of food-nutrient-drug interactions?
saqs.a: The elderly, malnourished, chronically ill, pregnant women, fetus and infants (and those with allergies/intolerances).

saqs.q: Why are drug interactions described as a 'preventable cause of morbidity'?
saqs.a: Because recognising them in advance (full drug history, knowing common interactions) lets the clinician avoid the reduced efficacy, side effects and toxicity they cause.
